112.s: Under the Rules, 1989, which body approves the environmental release and commercial use of GM crops?
112.x: GEAC under MoEFCC approves environmental release and commercial use; RCGM under DBT only monitors research and advises GEAC.

112.s: Field trials of GM crops in India are conducted as:
112.x: GM field trials are run as Biosafety Research Level trials, BRL-I and BRL-II.

112.s: Which of the following is NOT one of the competent authorities under the Rules, 1989?
112.x: The six competent authorities are RDAC, IBSC, RCGM, GEAC, SBCC and DLC; FSSAI is not one of them.

112.s: Since 2010, what has been mandatory for conducting GM crop field trials?
112.x: Since 2010 a State NOC is mandatory for field trials, and several States refuse it.

112.s: Which committee under the Rules, 1989 can inspect, investigate and take punitive action at the State level?
112.x: The SBCC acts at State level with powers to inspect, investigate and punish; DLC monitors at district level.

112.s: Consider the following statements and choose the correct ones using the codes given below : A . The flavr-savr tomato was the first genetically engineered crop product to be commercialised. B . Ripe fruits of flavr-savr remain firm for longer duration and can be transported to market after vine-ripening. C . Ripe fruits of flavr-savr have colour but not the full array of vine ripened tomato flavours. Code :
112.x: The flavr-savr tomato was the first commercially grown genetically engineered food to be granted a license for human consumption. The novel variety was developed by insertion of an additional copy of the PG (Polygalacturonase) encoding gene in the “antisense” orientation, resulting in reduced translation of the endogenous PG messenger RNA (mRNA). The antisense PG gene is essentially reverse copy of part of the native tomato PG gene that suppresses the expression of endogenous PG enzyme prior to the onset of fruit ripening. Flavr-savr tomatoes have improved harvest and processing properties that allow the transgenic tomatoes to remain longer on the vine to develop their natural flavour, maintain firmness for shipping and produce a thicker consistency in processing.

112.s: Genetically modified, Bt Brinjal is developed for :
Bt brinjal was developed for resistance against the:
112.x: Bt brinjal was developed for resistance to the fruit and shoot borer insect.
112.tq: Match the crop with its target pest rather than with another Bt crop’s pest.
xs: **Bt brinjal** was developed for resistance to the **fruit and shoot borer** (PYQ) — option **(3)** is correct.
**Bollworm** resistance is **Bt cotton**'s trait; **polygalacturonase** relates to **Flavr Savr**.
xa: Developer: **Mahyco** with **UAS Dharwad** and **TNAU**.
GEAC recommended release **2009**; **Jairam Ramesh**'s moratorium **2010**.
Gene: **Cry1Ac** from Bt.

112.s: The barnase-barstar genes used in GM mustard DMH-11 come from:
112.x: Barnase-barstar comes from Bacillus amyloliquefaciens; Bacillus thuringiensis is the source of Bt genes. DMH-11 was developed by Delhi University.
xa: Higher yield **25-30%**.
GEAC cleared environmental release in **2022**; held up under **Supreme Court** review.
Herbicide fears: DMH-11 carries the **bar gene**.

112.s: Which statement correctly describes Bollgard II cotton?
o: It uses the barnase-barstar system from Bacillus amyloliquefaciens
It contains only the antisense polygalacturonase gene
It contains Cry1Ac and Cry2Ab from Bacillus thuringiensis
It produces beta-carotene using daffodil genes alone
112.x: Bollgard II cotton contains Cry1Ac and Cry2Ab genes sourced from Bacillus thuringiensis. The other options describe Flavr Savr, Golden Rice or GM mustard.
112.tq: Distinguish similar GM crop technologies by their gene combinations.
xs: **Bollgard II** contains **Cry1Ac and Cry2Ab from Bacillus thuringiensis** — option **(3)** is correct.
**Barnase-barstar** = **GM mustard DMH-11**; **antisense polygalacturonase** = **Flavr Savr**; **beta-carotene** = **Golden Rice**.
xa: **Bollgard I** has only **Cry1Ac**; **Bollgard** = GM technology (PYQ).
Bt cotton trait: **bollworm** resistance.
Bt cotton approved **March 2002** — **only GM crop commercially cultivated**.

112.s: Golden Rice is designed to enhance the biosynthesis of:
o: Beta-carotene, a precursor of Vitamin A
112.x: Golden Rice is designed for beta-carotene biosynthesis, linked to Vitamin A nutrition.
112.tq: Match the product’s popular name with its intended nutritional trait.
xs: **Golden Rice** enhances **beta-carotene, a precursor of Vitamin A** (PYQ) — option **(3)** is correct.
**Cry toxins** = **Bt cotton**; **barnase** = **DMH-11**; **polygalacturonase** relates to **Flavr Savr** tomato.
xa: Genes from **daffodil** and a **soil bacterium**.
**Flavr Savr**: first commercial GM food (USA, **1994**).
Bt cotton genes: **Cry1Ac**, **Cry2Ab**.

112.s: Bt brinjal carries which gene against the fruit and shoot borer?
112.x: Bt brinjal uses the Cry1Ac gene against the fruit and shoot borer.

112.s: The Flavr Savr tomato achieved delayed ripening using:
112.x: Flavr Savr used antisense polygalacturonase for delayed ripening.

112.s: What are the states in which farmers defied the government and started cultivating Bt cotton and Bt brinjal?
112.x: Farmers in Maharashtra and Haryana were reported to have openly defied government restrictions and cultivated unapproved Bt cotton and Btbrinjal varieties in protest against regulatory delays.

112.s: In July 2024, the Supreme Court's ruling on GM mustard DMH-11 was a:
o: Dismissal of the case as withdrawn
112.x: The July 2024 verdict was split, though both judges directed the Centre to frame a national GM crop policy; GEAC had cleared its environmental release in 2022.
xa: **DMH-11** = hybrid seed system (**barnase-barstar**), **25-30%** higher yield; **Delhi University**.
Its commercial use is held up under **Supreme Court** review.
Herbicide fears: **DMH-11** carries the **bar gene**.

112.s: Which State is recognised as the leading Bt cotton-growing State in India?
112.x: Maharashtra is identified as the leading Bt cotton State.
112.tq: Test the crop-State association directly using a nearby cotton-growing State as the distractor.
xs: **Maharashtra** is the leading Bt cotton State (PYQ) — option **(3)** is correct.
Punjab, Gujarat and Telangana are not named as the leader in the notes.
xa: Bt cotton approved **March 2002**: three **MAHYCO** hybrids.
Area **12.5 million ha**, **over 90%** of cotton area.
Trait: **bollworm** resistance via **Cry1Ac**/**Cry2Ab**.

112.s: The Supreme Court-appointed Technical Expert Committee of 2013 recommended:
o: A 10-year moratorium on GM field trials
112.x: The 2013 Technical Expert Committee recommended a 10-year moratorium on field trials.

112.s: GEAC cleared the environmental release of GM mustard DMH-11 in:
112.x: GEAC cleared DMH-11 in 2017 but the Ministry withheld it; environmental release was cleared on 18 October 2022.

112.s: What is the primary environmental concern associated with Genetically Modified (GM) crops?
112.x: A major environmental concern with GM crops is gene flow/cross-pollination with wild relatives or non-GM varieties, which can spread engineered traits and cause loss of genetic purity.

112.s: Which one of the following technologies has been flagged for raising concerns about biodiversity?
112.x: Genetic modification is the technology flagged for biodiversity concerns (APPSC-GS 2023), through gene flow, monoculture and loss of diversity. Drip irrigation, solar panels and rainwater harvesting are not flagged this way.
xs: **Genetic modification of crops** is flagged for **biodiversity concerns** (APPSC-GS **2023**) — option **(2)** is correct.
Drip irrigation, rooftop solar and rainwater harvesting are not flagged this way.
xa: Concerns: gene flow, **monoculture**, loss of diversity, **genetic homogenisation**.
Primary environmental concern: **cross-pollination** to non-GM crops.
Resistance also stems from control by **big seed companies** holding patents.

112.s: Which of the following is NOT listed as an environmental or health risk of GM crops?
112.x: Insect resistance, harm to non-target organisms, weediness, genetic homogenisation, toxicity, allergenicity and antibiotic resistance are listed risks; ozone depletion is not a GM-crop risk.
xa: Primary environmental concern: **gene flow/cross-pollination**.
Reasons for resistance: **monoculture**, loss of diversity, control by **patent-holding seed companies**.
Herbicide-tolerance fears: **DMH-11** carries the **bar gene**.

112.s: Approval of a GM product in India may take about 7–10 years, compared with about ____ globally.
112.x: Overlapping mandates of DBT, GEAC, CDSCO, FSSAI and NBA and the lack of a biosafety liability law mean 7–10 years in India against 3–5 years globally.
xa: ⚠ Criticism: multi-layered regulation **delays approvals yet lacks a liability law**.
**BioE3 Policy 2024**: **single-window clearance** + regulatory sandboxes.
**BRAI Bill 2013** (single regulator) **lapsed**.

112.s: GM mustard DMH-11 also carries herbicide tolerance through the:
112.x: DMH-11 carries the bar gene, which gives herbicide tolerance and fuels public resistance.

112.s: Which genome-editing category is transgenic and remains under full GM regulatory control in India?
112.x: SDN-3 inserts foreign DNA and stays fully regulated; SDN-1 and SDN-2 make small edits without foreign DNA and are exempt under the 2022 guidelines.

112.s: Pusa Rice DST1 is associated with which of the following traits and editing features?
o: Insect resistance; insertion of a Bt toxin gene by SDN-2
Drought and salinity tolerance; DST gene knockout by SDN-1
Higher phosphate uptake; insertion of a foreign bacterial gene
Vitamin A enrichment; mitochondrial gene replacement
112.x: Pusa Rice DST1 is an edited form of MTU1010, designed for drought and salinity tolerance through DST gene knockout using SDN-1.
112.tq: Combine the crop, trait and technical method instead of relying on the variety name alone.
xs: **Pusa Rice DST1** gives **drought and salinity tolerance** by **DST gene knockout via SDN-1** — option **(2)** is correct.
It is a **CRISPR-Cas9** edit of **MTU1010**, with **no foreign DNA** — so not Bt insertion, foreign bacterial gene or vitamin A.
xa: Yield **10-30%** higher under stress; set for commercial launch (**1 Sep 2026**).
Developer: **ICAR-IARI, Delhi**.
**Phosphate uptake** rice is **NIPGR**'s; **vitamin A** rice is **Golden Rice**.

112.s: For genome-edited crops covered by the SDN-1 and SDN-2 exemption, which approval route is indicated?
o: IBC approval without the GEAC route
Only approval from the State Pollution Control Board
Approval from the Supreme Court after public consultation
112.x: Genome-edited crops covered by the SDN-1 and SDN-2 exemption can skip the GEAC route and require IBC approval.
112.tq: Ask which authority performs the relevant regulatory function instead of assuming every biotechnology product follows the GEAC route.
xs: Genome-edited crops under the SDN-1/SDN-2 exemption need only **IBC approval** and **skip the GEAC** route — option **(1)** is correct.
No State Pollution Board or Supreme Court route is involved.
xa: **IBSC** now clears **genome-edited crops** (Dec **2025**).
**2022 guidelines** exempt **SDN-1/SDN-2** (no foreign DNA).
**SDN-3** (transgenic) remains under full GM control.

112.s: Pusa Rice DST1 was set for commercial launch as India’s first genome-edited rice and was to be regulated like:
112.x: Pusa Rice DST1 was described as India’s first genome-edited rice for commercial launch and was to be regulated like a conventional crop.
112.tq: Test the regulatory classification rather than the biological trait.
xs: **Pusa Rice DST1**, an **SDN-1** edit with no foreign DNA, is treated like **a conventional crop** — option **(1)** is correct.
SDN-1/SDN-2 crops are **exempt** from GMO rules (**2022** guidelines) and **skip GEAC**.
xa: Developer: **ICAR-IARI**; edit of **DST gene** in **MTU1010**.
**Pusa DST1/Kamala** = first genome-edited rice; commercial launch (**1 Sep 2026**).
⚠ GE exemption criticised as a **back door**.

112.s: Pusa Rice DST1 was produced by an SDN-1 knockout of which gene?
112.x: Pusa Rice DST1 is an SDN-1 DST gene knockout in MTU1010, giving drought and salinity tolerance.

112.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Statement-I: India does not import apples from the United States of America.
2. Statement-II: In India, the law prohibits the import of Genetically Modified food without the approval of the competent authority. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct
112.x: Statement I is incorrect: Following the June 2023 decision to resolve six WTO disputes between the US and India through Mutually Agreed Solutions, India lifted additional duties on eight US-origin products, including apples, walnuts, and almonds. As a result, imports of American apples have increased significantly. Statement II is correct: The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 prohibits import, manufacture, use or sale of GM food without FSSAI's approval.

112.s: Regulation of genetically modified food, including its import, in India rests on which law?
o: Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001
112.x: GM food is governed by the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, with the FSSAI GM food framework of 2024; import of GM food without approval of the competent authority is prohibited. The EPA governs GMO release, the PPVFR Act plant varieties, and the Patents Act patents.
xs: GM food, including imports, rests on the **Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006** — option **(2)** is correct.
The **EPA 1986** governs GMO release (GEAC), the **PPVFR Act 2001** plant varieties, and the **Patents Act** patents.
xa: The law **prohibits GM food import without approval**.
**FSSAI GM food framework 2024**: approval of the **competent authority**.
July **2024**: SC **split verdict** on GM mustard; Centre told to frame a **national policy on GM crops**.

112.s: From 1 March 2021, imported major food crops into India need a:
112.x: Since 1 March 2021, imported major food crops must carry a 'non-GM cum GM-free' certificate.

112.s: India's draft GM labelling applies to foods containing GM ingredients of:
112.x: The draft labelling rule covers foods with 1% or more GM ingredient.

112.s: The Biotechnology Regulatory Authority of India (BRAI) Bill, 2013 proposed:
o: A ban on all GM crops
A separate patent office for seeds
A GM approval committee in every State
112.x: The BRAI Bill proposed a single biotechnology regulator but lapsed with the 15th Lok Sabha.
xa: **BioE3 Policy 2024** now proposes **single-window clearance** + **regulatory sandboxes**.
Overlapping regulators: **DBT, GEAC, CDSCO, FSSAI, NBA**.
GM approval takes **7-10 years** vs **3-5** globally.

112.s: Which policy proposes single-window clearance and regulatory sandboxes in the biotechnology sector?
112.x: The BioE3 Policy, 2024 proposes single-window clearance and regulatory sandboxes.
112.tq: Identify the policy by pairing its year with its distinctive regulatory features.
xs: The **BioE3 Policy, 2024** proposes **single-window clearance and regulatory sandboxes** — option **(3)** is correct.
**BRAI** was a **Bill (2013)** that **lapsed**, not an Act.
xa: **FSSAI GM food framework** is also of **2024**.
Delays from overlapping mandates: **7-10 years** for approval.
⚠ India has **no biosafety liability law**.

112.s: The BRAI Bill, 2013 lapsed with the end of the:
112.x: The BRAI Bill proposed a single biotech regulator and lapsed with the 15th Lok Sabha.

112.s: In July 2024, which body directed the Centre to frame a national GM crop policy?
112.x: In its July 2024 split verdict on DMH-11, both Supreme Court judges directed the Centre to frame a national GM crop policy.

112.s: A genetically engineered form of brinjal, known as the Bt-Brinjal, has been developed. The objective of this is
o: To improve its taste and nutritive qualities
112.x: Bt Brinjal is a genetically engineered variety of brinjal developed to provide resistance against insect pests, particularly the Eggplant Fruit and Shoot Borer, which is a major pest affecting brinjal crops. In this variety, a gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis is inserted into the brinjal plant. This gene produces a protein that is toxic to specific insect pests, thereby protecting the crop from damage

112.s: A genetically engineered form of brinjal, known as the Bt brinjal has been developed. The objective of this is:
o: To improve its taste and nutritive qualities
112.x: Bt brinjal is a transgenic brinjal created by inserting a gene ‘Cry 1 Ac’ from the soil bacterium ‘Bacillus thuringiensis’ into brinjal. Bt brinjal has been developed to give resistance against lepidopteran insects like the brinjal shoot-borer Leucinodes orbonalis and fruit-borer Helicoverpa armigera. Bt brinjal has generated much debate in India. The promoters say that Bt brinjal will be beneficial to small farmers because it is insect resistant, increases yields etc. On the other hand, concerns about Bt brinjal relates to its possible adverse impact on human health and bio-safety, livelihoods and biodiversity. In India, Bt brinjal was developed by the Maharashtra Hybrid Seeds Co. (Mahyco). Despite the conduct of field trials from 2002-2006, a moratorium was issued in October, 2009 and a government ban was implemented in February, 2010.

112.s:
What are the reasons for the people’s resistance to the introduction of Bt brinjal in India?
1. Bt brinjal is created by inserting a gene from soil fungus into its genome.
2. The seeds of Bt brinjal are terminator seeds and therefore, the farmers have to buy the seeds before every season from the seed companies.
3. There is an apprehension that the consumption of Bt brinjal may have adverse impact on health.
4. There is some concern that the introduction of Bt brinjal may have adverse effect on the biodiversity.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
Which provision of the Patents Act excludes plants, animals, seeds and essentially biological processes from patentability while permitting patenting of microbial processes?
112.x: Section 3(j) excludes plants, animals, seeds and essentially biological processes from patentability, while microbial processes can be patented.
112.tq: Distinguish closely numbered statutory provisions by their subject matter.
xs: **Section 3(j)** excludes **plants, animals, seeds and essentially biological processes**, but **microbial processes** can be patented — option **(1)**.
**Section 3(d)** is the anti-**evergreening** clause (new form of a known substance).
xa: UPSC **2019**: a biological process to create a seed **cannot** be patented; plant varieties **not eligible**.
**IPAB** existed then; abolished **2021**.
Plant varieties are protected instead by the **PPVFR Act 2001**.

112.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Section 3(d) of the Patents Act?
o: It bars a patent for a new form of a known substance unless it shows enhanced efficacy
It is meant to block evergreening
In Novartis v Union of India (2013), the Glivec rejection was upheld under Section 3(j), not 3(d)
Section 3(j), a different clause, excludes plants, animals and seeds
112.x: The Supreme Court upheld the Glivec (imatinib) rejection under Section 3(d); Section 3(j) deals with plants, animals, seeds and essentially biological processes.
xa: **Section 3(j)**: plants, animals, seeds and **essentially biological processes** are not patentable; **microbial processes** can be.
**PPVFR Act 2001** protects plant varieties and **farmers' rights**.
**PepsiCo potato case (2019)** over **FL-2027 (FC5)**; registration revoked in **2021**.

112.s: Under the PPV&FR Act, 2001, farmers are NOT allowed to sell:
112.x: Farmers may save, use, sow, resow, exchange, share and sell farm produce including seed, but not branded seed of protected varieties.
xa: The Act **bars registration** of varieties carrying **GURT**.
**PepsiCo potato case (2019)**: **FL-2027 (FC5)**; PPVFR Authority revoked its registration (**2021**).
⚠ Plant varieties are **not eligible** for patents under **Section 3(j)** — the PPVFR Act protects them instead.

112.s: In the FL-2027 (FC5) potato variety case, PepsiCo sued farmers of which State?
112.x: PepsiCo sued Gujarat farmers, later withdrew the suits, and the PPVFR Authority revoked the variety's registration in 2021.
xa: Farmers may save, resow, exchange and sell seed — but **not branded seed**.
**PPVFR Act 2001** protects plant varieties and **farmers' rights**.
**IPAB** was abolished in **2021**.

112.s: Which of the following is an objection raised by farmers against GURT or terminator seeds?
112.x: Farmers object to dependence on companies, recurring seed costs and the loss of seed-saving.

112.s: Which one of the following statements about the PPVFR Act and GURT is correct?
o: The Act mandates registration of all varieties carrying GURT.
The Act bars registration of varieties carrying GURT.
The Act has no provision concerning GURT.
The Act permits registration only when farmers cannot save seed.
112.x: The PPVFR Act bars registration of varieties carrying Genetic Use Restriction Technology. This reflects concerns over seed dependency and loss of farmers' seed-saving rights.
112.tq: Watch for the reversed legal relationship between a statute and a controversial technology.
xs: The **PPVFR Act bars registration of varieties carrying GURT** — option **(2)** is correct.
So it neither mandates such registration nor is silent on GURT.
xa: GURT/**terminator seeds** yield **sterile seeds** → fresh seed every season.
Farmers' rights: **save, use, sow, resow, exchange, share, sell** seed — not **branded seed**.
**PPVFR Act 2001** (UPPSC **2021**).

112.s: In Novartis v Union of India (2013), the Supreme Court upheld the rejection of a patent on:
112.x: The SC upheld rejection of the Glivec (imatinib) patent under Section 3(d), which blocks evergreening.

112.s: The US patent on turmeric for wound healing was revoked after a challenge by:
112.x: The 1995 US turmeric patent was revoked after CSIR challenged it.

112.s: India won the neem biopiracy case at the:
112.x: India won the neem (anti-fungal) case at the European Patent Office.

112.s: The 1997 US patent on basmati rice, challenged by CSIR, was held by:
112.x: RiceTec of the USA held the 1997 basmati patent; key claims were disallowed after CSIR's challenge.

112.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
112.x: Hoodia (P57) is an appetite suppressant shared with the San people. Turmeric was for wound healing, neem anti-fungal and basmati was RiceTec's patent.

112.s: The Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (2001) was set up by:
112.x: TKDL was created in 2001 by CSIR and the Ministry of AYUSH.

112.s: TKDL helps against biopiracy mainly by giving patent offices:
112.x: TKDL gives patent offices prior-art evidence that the knowledge already exists.

112.s: The expression “designer babies” is most directly associated with which ethical debate?
o: Use of adult stem cells for tissue repair
Inspection of laboratories handling moderate-risk agents
Protection of traditional knowledge from patent claims
Use of genetic technologies to select or modify desired human traits
112.x: “Designer babies” refers to the ethical concern that genetic technologies could be used to select or modify desired traits in human offspring.
112.tq: Translate the ethical term into its underlying biotechnology application.
xs: **"Designer babies"** refers to the **use of genetic technologies to select or modify desired human traits** — option **(4)** is correct.
It is tied to **germline editing**, an ethical issue in bioethics.
xa: Other ethical issues: **three-parent baby** technique, **animal cloning welfare**, **informed consent**.
**He Jiankui** (China, **2018**): human embryo editing — **"CRISPR babies"**.
**UNESCO's International Bioethics Committee** monitors genome-editing ethics.

112.s: Lethal agents with no cure, such as Ebola, require which biosafety level?
112.x: Such agents need BSL-4; BSL-2 is for moderate-risk agents and BSL-3 for serious airborne agents such as TB.
xa: **BSL-4**: lethal agents with no cure (e.g. **Ebola**); India: **NIV Pune**.
**DBT** handles **biocontainment**; **NCDC** handles surveillance.
**Cartagena Protocol**: adopted **2000**, in force **2003**.

112.s: The National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017 were issued jointly by which organisations?
112.x: The National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017 were issued through the ICMR-DBT framework and provide ethical and regulatory guidance.
112.tq: Identify the institutions directly associated with the named guidelines.
xs: The **National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017** were issued jointly by **ICMR and DBT** — option **(3)** is correct.
They provide an **ethical + regulatory framework**.
xa: Stem cell sources: **embryonic**, **adult**, **umbilical cord blood**, **iPSC**.
**UNESCO's International Bioethics Committee** is the **global monitor** of genome-editing ethics.
**rDNA Guidelines** are also of **2017**.

112.s: Human embryo editing associated with the birth of the so-called “CRISPR babies” was carried out by He Jiankui in:
112.x: He Jiankui’s human embryo-editing experiment in China became widely associated with the “CRISPR babies” controversy in 2018.
112.tq: Discriminate between closely placed country-year combinations.
xs: **He Jiankui** carried out **human embryo editing** ("CRISPR babies") in **China in 2018** — option **(1)** is correct.
**2000** (Colombia) is the **Cartagena Protocol**; **1994** (USA) the **Flavr Savr** tomato; **2017** India's **stem cell guidelines**.
xa: Ethical issues: **germline editing**, **"designer babies"**.
**UNESCO's International Bioethics Committee** = global monitor.
**National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017** (**ICMR-DBT**).

112.s: Cartagena, after which the Protocol on Biosafety is named, is a city in:
112.x: Cartagena is in Colombia; the Protocol is supplementary to the Convention on Biological Diversity.

112.s: Which Indian law criminalises biological weapons?
112.x: The WMD Act, 2005 criminalises biological weapons in India; India is also a Party to the BWC (opened 1972, in force 1975).
xa: **DBT** = biocontainment; **NCDC** = surveillance.
**Global Health Security Index (2023)**: India **66th**.
Gap: **no unified national biosecurity framework**.

112.s: Which of the following is identified as a gap in India’s biosecurity system?
o: Non-membership in the Biological Weapons Convention
Absence of any institution concerned with disease surveillance
Complete prohibition of all genetic engineering research
Absence of a unified national biosecurity framework
112.x: The stated gap is the absence of a unified national biosecurity framework, with laws also lagging behind synthetic biology and gene editing. India is a party to the BWC.
112.tq: Identify the stated institutional gap while rejecting absolute distractors.
xs: The gap is the **absence of a unified national biosecurity framework** — option **(4)** is correct.
India **is a Party** to the **BWC**, and **NCDC** does surveillance — so options (1), (2) are wrong; research is not prohibited.
xa: Laws also **lag synthetic biology and gene editing**.
**Global Health Security Index (2023)**: India **66th**.
**BWC**: opened **1972**, in force **1975**.

112.s: The Biological Weapons Convention entered into force in:
112.x: The BWC was opened in 1972 and entered into force in 1975; India is a Party.

112.s: Serious airborne agents such as TB are handled at which biosafety level?
112.x: BSL-3 is for serious airborne agents like TB; BSL-4 is for lethal agents with no cure like Ebola.

113.s: The size of the nanoparticle ranges between :
The most important property of nanomaterials is –
113.x: Friction is the most important property of nanomaterials.

113.s: A particle having at least one dimension less than 10–7 metre, is known as
113.x: Among the above options, nanoparticles are particles having at least one dimension less than 10–7 metre. According to the definition, a nano-object have one of its characteristic dimensions to be in the range 1-100 nm (10–9 – 10–7m) to be classified as a nanoparticle.

113.s: Besides quantum effects, the unusual properties of nanomaterials arise mainly from their:
113.x: Quantum effects and a very high surface-area-to-volume ratio give nanomaterials enhanced reactivity and unusual optical and electrical behaviour.
xa: They also show different **optical/electrical** behaviour.
Nanoparticle size: **1-100 nm** (APPSC **2018**).
**1 nm** = one billionth (**10^-9**) of a metre.

113.s: One nanometre equals:
113.x: 1 nm is one billionth of a metre, 10^-9 m; nanoparticles span 10^-9 to 10^-7 m.

113.s: Which one of the following pairs is not correctly matched?
113.x: Dry Ice – We can simply say that dry ice is solid carbon dioxide CO2. It is used as a cooling agent. Mustard gas – It is used as a strong chemical weapon. This mortally chemical affects skin, leering eye, lungs and D.N.A. which affects the cells most. After 1-6 hours the symptoms seem to be visible. Graphene is frequently in the news recently. What is its importance?
1. It is a two-dimensional material and has good electrical conductivity.
2. It is one of the thinnest but strongest materials tested so far.
3. It is entirely made of silicon and has high optical transparency.
4. It can be used as 'conducting electrodes' required for touch screens, LCDs and organic LEDs.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
113.x: Statement 1, 2 and 4 are correct, and statement 3 is incorrect: Graphene is a single layer (monolayer) of pure carbon, tightly bound in a hexagonal honeycomb lattice. It is an allotrope of carbon. It is extracted from graphite. Graphite is arranged in a 3D crystalline manner, whereas graphene is a 2D crystal, only an atom thick. • Properties: Graphene is the thinnest (one-atom-thick) compound known.  It is the lightest material known and the strongest compound discovered (between 100-300 times stronger than steel, and harder than diamond).  It is an excellent conductor of electricity and has high thermal conductivity.  It is flexible, transparent, and has a large surface area. • Applications: Due to its high electrical conductivity, optical transparency and flexibility, graphene is ideal for conducting electrodes in touch screens, LCDs, and organic LEDs (OLEDs).  Biomedical industry: It can be used for targeted drug delivery, 'smart' implants, etc.  Automobile industry: Graphene is highly inert and so can act as a corrosion barrier between oxygen and water diffusion.  Potential alternative to lithium-ion batteries: It can be used to develop smaller, slimmer batteries with higher capacity, faster charging, and increased longevity than traditional batteries.

113.x: Statement 1 is correct: Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) are one of the most significant nano-allotropes of carbon. These are onedimensional tubes or cylindrical nanostructures composed of carbon atoms. Carbon nanotubes are essentially rolled graphene nanosheets with bonded carbon atoms. The unique carbon-carbon bonding and cylindrical structure give carbon nanotubes their exceptional strength. CNTs can be used in drug delivery systems due to their ability to be functionalized with therapeutic agents, proteins, and antigens. They can penetrate biological membranes and deliver drugs or other therapeutic agents directly to targeted cells, enhancing treatment efficiency and minimizing side effects. Statement 2 is incorrect: While CNTs exhibit excellent mechanical properties and biocompatibility, their application in creating artificial blood capillaries is not well-established. Challenges such as biocompatibility concerns, potential toxicity, and the complexity of mimicking the intricate structure and function of natural blood vessels make this application impractical at present. Statement 3 is correct: CNTs are highly effective for the development of biochemical sensors due to their sensitivity, high electrical conductivity, and ability to detect a wide range of biochemical substances. These sensors can detect minute changes in chemical or biological environments, making them useful in diagnostics, environmental monitoring, and healthcare. 113.x: Graphene is an allotrope of Carbon consisting of a single layer of atoms arranged in a honeycomb nanostructure. It is an extremely good electrical conductor and is highly resistant to heat and acids. The two scientists of Manchester University-Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov properly isolated and characterized it in 2004. The both were awarded Nobel Prize in Physics in 2010 for groundbreaking experiments regarding the two-dimensional material graphene. They extracted Graphene from a piece of Graphite. Graphene is a bi-dimensional element and due to this quality, controlling electricity is easier in it than a tri-dimensional element. Graphene is not only very thin but also strongest among all the materials tested so far. It is almost transparent, despite, being so dense that the smallest gas molecule cannot pass through it. It can be used as 'conducting electrodes' required for touchscreens, LCDs and organic LEDs. Graphene can be used to make faster computer chips, communication devices etc.

The extreme case of this process of size reduction in which all three dimensions reach the low nanometer range is called a quantum dot.

114.s: Which part of human body is infected by the virus causing Japanese encephalitis?
114.x: Japanese encephalitis (JE) is an infection of the brain caused by the Japanese Encepthalitis Virus (JEV). JEV is the main cause of viral encephalitis in many countries of Asia with an estimated 68,000 clinical cases every year. While most infections result in little or no symptoms, occasional inflammation of the brain occurs. In these cases, symptoms may include headache, vomiting, fever, confusion and seizures. This occurs about 5 to 15 days after infection.

(Pre) (Re-Exam) 2024 Ans. (c) While Anopheles mosquitoes are well-known as vectors for malaria, they can also be vectors for certain types of encephalitis. Japanese Encephalitis Virus (JEV) is a significant cause of encephalitis in Asia, and while Culex mosquitoes are the primary vectors, Anopheles mosquitoes, such as Anopheles subpictus, have been identified as vectors in specific regions where they are more abundant. Anopheles mosquitoes can also carry other encephalitis viruses, such as St. Louis Encephalitis Virus (SLEV) and Eastern Equine Encephalitis Virus (EEE). Anopheles mosquitoes are also vectors of filariasis in some regions, particularly in rural areas of Asia and Africa. In fact, the World Health Organization (WHO) notes that lymphatic filariasis is transmitted by various mosquito species, including Anopheles. Other important vectors for filariasis include Culex and Aedes mosquitoes. Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.

114.x: Wolbachia is one of the world's most common types of bacteria, present in 50-60% of all insect species, including bees, beetles, butterflies, moths, and fruit flies. Wolbachia blocks viruses like dengue, chikungunya and Zika from growing in the bodies of Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. This means that Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes have a reduced ability to transmit viruses to people. When Wolbachia is established in a mosquito population it results in a decreasing incidence of dengue, Zika, chikungunya etc. World Mosquito Program's Wolbachia method can protect communities from mosquito-borne diseases without posing risk to natural ecosystems.

114.s: Which of the following is not a Zoonotic disease?
114.x: Zoonotic disease is an infectious disease caused by a pathogen (an infectious agent, such as a bacterium, virus, parasite or prion) that has jumped from an animal (usually a vertebrate) to a human. Rabies, Plague and SARS (Severe acute respiratory syndrome) are zoonotic diseases. Mucormycosis is not a zoonotic disease. Mucormycosis (previously called zygomycosis) is a serious but rare fungal infection caused by a group of molds called mucormycetes. These molds live throughout the environment. Mucormycosis mainly affects people who have health problems or take medicines that lower the body's ability to fight germs and sickness. It is also known as black fungus. Symptoms depend on where in the body the infection occurs. It most commonly infects the nose, sinuses, eye, and brain resulting in a runny nose, one-sided facial swelling and pain, headache, fever, blurred vision, bulging or displacement of the eye (proptosis), and tissue death. Other forms of disease may infect the lungs, stomach and intestines, and skin.

2. When cysts develop in the brain, the condition is referred to as neuro-cysticercosis (NCC).
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
114.x: The term taeniasis refers to intestinal infection with tapeworms. Three parasite species cause taeniasis in humans. Taenia solium (pork tapeworm), Taenia saginata (beef tapeworm) and Taenia asiatica (Asian tapeworm). Only T. solium causes major health problems. T. solium taeniasis is acquired by humans through the ingestion of the parasite's larval cysts (cysticerci) in undercooked and infected pork. Humans can also become infected with T. solium eggs due to poor hygiene (via the fecal-oral route) or ingesting contaminated food or water. Ingested T. solium eggs develop to larvae (called cysticerci) in various organs of the human body. When they enter the central nervous system (i.e. in brain and spinal cord), they can cause neurological symptoms (neurocysticercosis), including epileptic seizures. Hence, both statements are correct.

114.s: Which of the following disease is related to Coronavirus?
114.x: Coronaviruses are a group of related RNA viruses that cause diseases in mammals and birds. In humans and birds, they cause respiratory tract infections that can range from mild to lethal. 114.s: Which of the following disease is not caused by a bacteria?
114.x: Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) is caused by infection with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). HIV infects T-helper cells, a type of T-lymphocytes which helps both B-lymphocytes (which produce antibodies) and other T-lymphocytes ( which kill cells infected by viruses) to carry out their functions. Neither type of lymphocyte can therefore operate and so the body’s immune system is rendered ineffective, not only against HIV but to other infections also. Due to this reason AIDS victims are frequently killed within a few years of developing the disease.

114.s: Which one of the following is not caused by infected mosquito bite :
114.x: Plague is an infectious disease caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which primarily affects wild rodents. It is spread from one rodent to another by fleas. Humans bitten by an infected flea usually develop a bubonic form of plague, which is characterized by a bubo i.e. a swelling of the lymph node draining the flea bite site. If the bacteria reach the lungs, the patient develops pneumonic plague. If diagnosed early, bubonic plague can be successfully treated with antibiotics. But in case of pneumonic plague, patients can die within 24 hours after infection.

114.s: The term antibiotic was coined by :
114.x: The term 'antibiotic' was first coined by Selman Waksman in 1942, to describe any substance produced by a microorganism that is antagonistic to the growth of other microorganisms. Selman Waksman is also known for his discovery of streptomycin and several other antibiotics. An antibiotic is a type of antimicrobial substance active against bacteria. It is the most important type of antibacterial agent for fighting bacterial infections, and antibiotic medications are widely used in the treatment and prevention of such infections.

114.s: Antibiotics are mostly obtained from :
114.x: Antibiotics are medicines that fight bacterial infections in people and animals. They work by killing the bacteria or by making it hard for the bacteria to grow and multiply. Antibiotics are mostly obtained from bacteria. Majority of antibiotics are produced by Streptomyces (and other actinomycetes) and various Bacillus species. Actinomycetes is the family of soil bacteria that has produced most of our antibiotics and other medically useful molecules. Many antibiotics are also obtained from other microorganisms, such as moulds and fungus. With advances in medicinal chemistry, most modern antibiotics are semisynthetic modifications of various natural compounds. However, some are also produced solely by chemical synthesis in the lab.

Some of the sulfa drugs are Sulfonamide antibiotics sulfadiazine, sulfasalazine, sulfisoxazole, sulfacetamide etc. Prontosil was the first sulfa drug discovered in 1932.

Chloramphenicol is also known as chloronitromycin. It is a broad-spectrum antibiotic drug used against serious infections such as typhoid fever.

Consider the following statements:
1. Statement-I: India's public sector health care system largely focuses on curative care with limited preventive, promotive and rehabilitative care.
2. Statement-II: Under India's decentralized approach to health care delivery, the States are primarily responsible for organizing health services. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for State-
Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct
115.x: Statement 1 is correct: India's public sector health care system largely focuses on curative care with limited preventive, promotive and rehabilitative care. This approach has led to several challenges and missed opportunities for improving public health outcomes. For example, over the past 40 years, India has experienced a significant shift in its health landscape, with non-communicable diseases (NCDs) becoming the country's biggest health crisis. NCDs, including heart diseases, cancer, chronic respiratory diseases, and diabetes, now account for around 66% of all deaths in India (2019 data), up from 25% in 1990. These diseases contribute to a substantial economic burden, with costs projected to reach ₹511 lakh crore ($6.2 trillion) by 2030. Statement 2 is correct: Under India's decentralized healthcare delivery approach, the states are primarily responsible for organizing health services. Both statements are correct, but Statement-II is not the correct explanation of Statement-I. The curative-centric nature of India's healthcare system stems from historical policy priorities, funding patterns, and infrastructure development, not from the constitutional division of responsibilities between the Centre and States.

116.x: Endemic – A disease regularly found in a particular place or among a particular group of a people and difficult to get rid of. Epidemic – A large number of cases of a particular disease happening in a given population within a short period of time. Pandemic – An infectious disease that has spread across a large region, for instance whole country, multiple continents or worldwide, affecting a substantial number of people. Epizootic – A disease that affects a large number of animals in some particular region within a short period of time.

**Endemic** = constant baseline; **pandemic** = across countries and continents; **epizootic** = among animals.

(ii) Intensified year-round Behaviour Change Communication (BCC) Campaign for : (a) improving compliance to Iron Folic Acid supplementation and deworming, (b) enhancing appropriate infant and young child feeding practices, (c) encouraging increase in intake of iron-rich food through diet diversity/quantity/frequency and/or fortified foods with focus on harnessing locally available resources, and (d) ensuring delayed cord clamping after delivery (by 3 minutes) in health facilities. (iii) Testing and treatment of anaemia, using digital methods and point of care treatment, with special focus on pregnant women and school-going adolescents. (iv) Addressing non-nutritional causes of anaemia in endemic pockets with special focus on malaria, haemoglobinopathies and fluorosis. Iodine, zinc and vitamin A only
118.x: The specified fortified rice contains iron, folic acid and vitamin B12 and is supplied through the PDS, ICDS and PM POSHAN.

AP's **Anna Amrutha Hastam** adds **iron and folic acid tablets** to meals.
NFHS-5 anaemia among children 6-59 months: **67.1%**.

118.s: PM POSHAN, launched in 2021, was renamed from which scheme?

118.x: Anna Amrutha Hastam provides a nutritious meal and iron-folic acid tablets to pregnant and lactating women through Anganwadis.

xs: **Anna Amrutha Hastam** (AP) gives a **nutritious meal** plus **iron and folic acid tablets** to **pregnant and lactating women** via **Anganwadis** — option **(3)** (APPSC 2019 PYQ).
**PMSMA, LaQshya, JSSK** are other maternal services listed in APSES 2024-25.

**JSY** had **1,76,966** beneficiaries (Apr-Dec 2024).

118.s: YSR Sampoorna Poshana Plus covers pregnant women, lactating mothers and children in how many tribal mandals?

119.s: India's National Health Accounts, prepared by NHATS under NHSRC, use which framework?
119.x: The NHA use the System of Health Accounts 2011 (with NHA Guidelines 2016); the first NHA was for 2013-14.
xa: The latest is the **10th edition** for **2022-23** (May 2026).
OOPE share of THE: **64.2%** → **43.4%**.

119.s: The government share of India's Total Health Expenditure rose from 28.6% in 2013–14 to:
119.x: The government share rose to 43.7%; 39.4% is the OOPE share during COVID-19.
xa: OOPE share fell from **64.2%** to **43.4%**.
**Social security expenditure** share rose from **6%** to **9.9%**.

119.s: During COVID-19, household out-of-pocket expenditure fell to what share of Total Health Expenditure?
119.x: OOPE fell to 39.4% of THE during COVID-19, when government health expenditure peaked; 28.6% was the government share in 2013–14.
xa: NHA is prepared by **NHATS under NHSRC**, first for **2013-14**.

119.s: Government Health Expenditure reached what percentage of GDP during the COVID peak in 2021–22?
119.x: GHE reached 1.84% of GDP during the COVID peak in 2021–22.
119.tq: Distinguish the exceptional COVID-year peak from the regular annual figures.
xs: GHE reached **1.84% of GDP** in **2021-22**, the **COVID peak** — option **(3)**.
xa: ⚠ OOPE **fell**, not rose, during COVID — to **39.4%** of THE.
Centre + States spent about **1.3% of GDP** in **2019-20** (Economic Survey 2021-22).

119.s: According to the Economic Survey 2021–22 context, Centre and States together spent approximately what percentage of GDP on health in 2019–20?
119.x: Centre and States together spent about 1.3% of GDP on health in 2019–20.
119.tq: Recall the approximate combined public-spending figure rather than the NHP target.
xs: Centre + States spent about **1.3% of GDP** on health in **2019-20** — option **(2)** (Economic Survey 2021-22).
**2.5%** is the **NHP 2017** target; **1.84%** was the **2021-22** COVID peak.
xa: On the new GDP base: **1.48%**.
The Centre's own spending is **~0.29% of GDP**.

119.s: The first National Health Accounts estimates in India were prepared for the year:
119.x: India's first NHA was for 2013-14.

119.s: According to NHA 2022-23, the share of social security expenditure in Total Health Expenditure was:
119.x: Social security's share rose from 6% (2013-14) to 9.9% (2022-23).

119.s: Which of the following statements regarding the National Health Policy, 2017 target is correct?
o: It targeted GHE of 2.5% of GDP by 2022, with the Centre contributing 60%.
It targeted GHE of 1.5% of GDP by 2025, with the States contributing 40%.
It targeted GHE of 2.5% of GDP by 2025, with the Centre contributing 40% of public spending.
It targeted GHE of 3% of GDP by 2030, with no specified Centre share.
119.x: NHP 2017 targeted Government Health Expenditure of 2.5% of GDP by 2025, with the Centre’s share intended to be 40% of public spending. The target was missed.
119.tq: Match the target year, percentage and Centre-share provision precisely.
xs: **NHP 2017** targeted GHE of **2.5% of GDP by 2025**, with the **Centre's share 40%** of public spending — option **(3)**.
The target was **missed** (30 Jan 2026).
xa: The Centre now spends only **~0.29% of GDP**.
GHE stood at **1.43%** of GDP in **2022-23**.
NHA 2022-23 and the parliamentary panel on the **'missing middle'** both confirm the target is unmet.

119.s: Which of the following pairs relating to the 15th Finance Commission health grants is correctly matched?
o: Coverage – only urban health and wellness centres
119.x: The 15th FC recommended ₹70,051 crore for 2021–26 through local governments, covering rural and building-less SCs/PHCs/CHCs too, not only urban HWCs.

119.s: The 15th Finance Commission recommended health grants of approximately what amount through local governments for the period 2021–2026?
119.x: The 15th Finance Commission recommended health grants amounting to ₹70,051 crore through local governments for 2021–2026.
119.tq: Use the exact figure and period to eliminate nearby numerical distractors.
xs: The **15th Finance Commission** gave **₹70,051 crore** of health grants through **local governments** for **2021-26** — option **(3)**.
The grants go to local bodies for primary-level and block-level health infrastructure.
xa: Components: **diagnostic infrastructure** for sub-centres/PHCs and **block public health units**.
Also **urban health and wellness centres**.
And **buildings for building-less SCs/PHCs/CHCs**.

119.s: Under the National Health Policy 2017, the Centre's share of public health spending was to be:
119.x: NHP 2017 set the Centre's share at 40% of public health spending, along with GHE of 2.5% of GDP by 2025.

119.s: Which of the following correctly represents the trend in OOPE as a share of Total Health Expenditure between 2013–14 and 2022–23?
119.x: OOPE declined from 64.2% of Total Health Expenditure in 2013–14 to 43.4% in 2022–23, although it remained about half of current health expenditure.
119.tq: Reject the reversed trend and distinguish total health expenditure from current health expenditure.
xs: Option (4) reverses it; **28.6%** is the 2013-14 government share.
xa: OOPE is still about **50% of current health expenditure** (NHA 2022-23).
⚠ During COVID OOPE **fell** to **39.4%** of THE.

119.s: Which of the following components account for over 50% of OOPE because they are generally not covered by insurance?
o: Only inpatient surgery and intensive care
Ambulance services and health education alone
119.x: Outpatient care, diagnostics and medicines account for over half of OOPE because insurance commonly does not cover them.
119.tq: Apply the coverage gap to identify the major sources of household spending.
xs: **Outpatient care, diagnostics and medicines** are **over 50%** of OOPE — option **(4)**.
They are the uncovered costs; inpatient care is what insurance mainly covers.
xa: Chronic NCDs keep households paying: **diabetes 11.4%**, **hypertension 35.5%** of adults.
Private outpatient medicine bills are about **6 times** those at **Jan Aushadhi**.
Fix suggested: more spending on **primary care** + **OPD cover**.

119.s: The term “missing middle” in the context of health financing refers to:
o: More than 40 crore Indians lacking financial protection
People covered simultaneously by both public and private insurance
The middle-income group receiving free medicines at public facilities
Households whose insurance claims are pending for less than one month
119.x: The “missing middle” refers to more than 40 crore Indians who lack adequate financial protection; NITI Aayog first flagged the term.
119.tq: Match the distinctive policy term with its precise population description.
xs: The **"missing middle"** = **40 crore+** Indians lacking **financial protection** — option **(1)**.
**NITI Aayog** first flagged the term; the parliamentary panel used it on **4 Sep 2026**.
xa: NSS 80th round: insurance covers **47.4%** rural and **44.3%** urban households.
Childbirth OOP: **₹37,630** private vs **₹2,299** public (over **16x**).
Government-financed insurance rose **2.5-fold** (**2017-18** to **2025**).

119.s: PM-JAY provides health cover of how much per family per year?
119.x: PM-JAY covers ₹5 lakh per family per year; ₹25 lakh is AP's Universal Health Policy cover.

119.s: In October 2024, PM-JAY was extended to all citizens aged 70 and above:
o: Only if not covered by any other scheme
119.x: The October 2024 extension covers all citizens aged 70+, irrespective of income, through the Ayushman Vay Vandana card.

119.s:
Consider the following statements about the 2024 PM-JAY extension for senior citizens:
1. Beneficiaries receive the Ayushman Vay Vandana card.
2. Members aged 70+ of already covered families get an extra ₹5 lakh top-up.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
119.x: Both are correct: the 70+ cover uses the Ayushman Vay Vandana card and gives a ₹5 lakh top-up to already covered families.

119.s: Which of the following is regarded as a criticism of insurance-led health financing models?
o: They provide universal outpatient coverage in all circumstances.
They increase coverage without necessarily increasing the availability of care.
They reduce coverage while automatically increasing the quality of care.
They eliminate the need for primary healthcare expenditure.
119.x: A stated criticism is that insurance-led models may expand coverage without a corresponding increase in actual care. Greater spending on primary care and outpatient care is suggested as part of the corrective approach.
119.tq: Distinguish nominal financial coverage from actual access to healthcare.
xs: Insurance-led models **increase coverage without increasing care** — option **(2)**.
The suggested fix is more spending on **primary care** plus **OPD cover**.
xa: Outpatient care, diagnostics and medicines = **over 50%** of OOPE, mostly uncovered.
Government-financed insurance grew **2.5-fold** but OOPE still ~**50%** of current health expenditure.
**Missing middle**: **40 crore+** lack protection.

119.s: Between 2017-18 and 2025, government-financed health insurance coverage in India rose by about:
119.x: NSS 80th round shows government-financed insurance up 2.5-fold.

119.s: According to NFHS-6, households with at least one insured member rose from 41.0% to:
119.x: NFHS-6 shows insured households rising from 41.0% to 60.2%.

119.s: How are medicines that are to be sold only on the prescription of recognised medical experts classified?
How many drugs have been deleted from the revised National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM) 2022?
Which of the following is NOT correct about the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA)?
o: It fixes ceiling prices of scheduled drugs
Scheduled drugs are those in the National List of Essential Medicines
Its price control operates under the Drugs Price Control Order, 2013
119.x: NPPA was established in 1997; 2013 is the year of the Drugs Price Control Order under which it fixes ceiling prices.
xa: **Free Drugs Service Initiative (NHM)**: free generic medicines; **DVDMS** handles procurement/inventory.
**Clinical Establishments Act 2010** adopted in only ~**11 states** and **6 UTs**.
Medicines are part of the **over 50%** of OOPE not covered by insurance.

119.s: The Clinical Establishments Act, adopted by only about 11 States and 6 UTs, was enacted in:
119.x: The Act dates to 2010; 2013 is the Drugs Price Control Order and 2017 the National Health Policy.
xa: **NPPA** was set up in **1997**.
Hospitalisation OOP rose sharply, especially in **private hospitals** (NSS 80th round).
Private childbirth costs **₹37,630** vs **₹2,299** public.

119.s: DVDMS is associated with which function in the public medicine-supply system?
o: Setting the list of essential surgical procedures
119.x: DVDMS manages drug procurement and inventory under the Free Drugs Service Initiative.
119.tq: Match the digital system with its operational function.
xs: **DVDMS** manages **drug procurement and inventory** — option **(2)**.
It works under the **Free Drugs Service Initiative (NHM)**, which provides free generic medicines at public facilities.
xa: **NPPA (1997)** fixes ceiling prices of scheduled (**NLEM**) drugs.
NPPA acts under the **Drugs Price Control Order, 2013**.
Private pharmacies dominate over **Jan Aushadhi**, with bills about **6 times** higher.

119.s: How many Jan Aushadhi Kendras had been opened by December 2025?
119.x: 17,990 Jan Aushadhi Kendras had opened by Dec 2025; 25,000 is the target for March 2027.

119.s: The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) was set up in:
119.x: NPPA was set up in 1997; it fixes ceiling prices under the Drugs Price Control Order 2013.

119.s: Dr. NTR Vaidya Seva, formerly known as YSR Aarogyasri, is primarily intended to provide which of the following?
o: Subsidised insurance exclusively for private-sector employees
Free crop insurance to small farmers
Pension support to retired government employees
Cashless health assurance to economically vulnerable families in Andhra Pradesh
119.x: Dr. NTR Vaidya Seva, earlier YSR Aarogyasri, is Andhra Pradesh’s flagship cashless health assurance scheme for economically vulnerable families.
119.tq: Directly identify the purpose of the flagship state scheme.
xs: **Dr. NTR Vaidya Seva** (earlier **YSR Aarogyasri**) is AP's flagship **cashless health assurance** for **economically vulnerable families** — option **(4)**.
It is not an employee-only, crop-insurance or pension scheme.
xa: It runs **in convergence with PM-JAY** (portability, wider empanelment).
**Mar 2026**: **five more critical cardiovascular procedures** added.
AP Budget 2024-25 BE: **₹4,000 Cr** for the Dr. NTR Vaidya Seva Trust.
AP households covered by all schemes: **70%**.

119.s: Dr. NTR Vaidya Seva in Andhra Pradesh is implemented in convergence with which scheme, enabling portability and wider empanelment?
119.x: The AP scheme runs in convergence with PM-JAY, providing portability and wider hospital empanelment.

119.s: Andhra Pradesh's Universal Health Policy (Sep 2025) provides cover of up to how much per family per year?
119.x: The policy offers up to ₹25 lakh per family per year covering all 3,257 procedures.

119.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Andhra Pradesh's Universal Health Policy (2025)?
o: Claims up to ₹2.5 lakh are handled through insurers
Employees under the Employee Health Scheme are included
Claims from ₹2.5 lakh to ₹25 lakh go through the NTR Vaidya Seva Trust
119.x: EHS employees are excluded from the Universal Health Policy; the other statements are correct.

119.s: Together with EHS, RSBY, ESIS and CGHS, AP's state health scheme covers about what share of AP households (2026)?
119.x: The state scheme with EHS, RSBY, ESIS and CGHS covers about 70% of AP households.

120.s: India's first National Health Policy was issued in:
120.x: India's National Health Policies came in 1983, 2002 and 2017.
xa: **India Newborn Action Plan**: **2014**.
**National Policy for Rare Diseases**: **2021**.
NHP 2017 target: public health spending **2.5% of GDP by 2025** — missed (**1.43%** in 2022-23).

120.s: The National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) and the National Urban Health Mission (NUHM) were launched respectively in:
120.x: NRHM was launched in 2005 and NUHM in 2013; together they form the National Health Mission.
xa: NRHM was asked in **APPSC 2023** PYQ.
NRHM goal: **accessible, affordable, quality care** for rural India.
NHM funding: **60:40**; NE and Himalayan states **90:10**.

120.s: The Indian Research Fund Association, the predecessor of the Indian Council of Medical Research, was established in:
120.x: The Indian Research Fund Association was established in 1911 and was later renamed the ICMR in 1949.
120.tq: Distinguish the founding year from the later renaming year.
xs: The **Indian Research Fund Association (IRFA)** was set up in **1911** — option **(2)**.
It was renamed **ICMR** in **1949**; **1948** is the year **WHO** was founded.
xa: ICMR is among the world's **oldest medical research bodies**.
ICMR consortia: **MERA India** (malaria), **India TB Research Consortium**, **India Hypertension Control Initiative**.
The **Medical Device and Diagnostic Mission Secretariat** reduces import dependence.

120.s: Which of the following best characterises the approach of the National Health Policy, 2017?
o: A private-sector-only approach to emergency care
An assurance-based approach with comprehensive primary care
An insurance-only approach without public-sector services
A disease-specific approach limited to communicable diseases
120.x: NHP 2017 adopted an assurance-based approach and envisaged comprehensive primary care rather than an insurance-only or disease-specific model.
120.tq: Identify the official policy approach while rejecting extreme alternatives such as “only” and “private-sector-only.”
xs: **NHP 2017** took an **assurance-based approach** with **comprehensive primary care** — option **(2)**.
Its primary care package covers **NCDs, mental health, geriatric and palliative care** via **Health and Wellness Centres** — not communicable diseases alone.
xa: Public hospitals: **free drugs, diagnostics + emergency care**.
Targets: **TFR 2.1 by 2025**; life expectancy **67.5 → 70 by 2025**.
⚠ Spending target **2.5% of GDP by 2025** was missed.

120.s: Along with increased public spending on health, the National Health Policy, 2002 emphasised:
o: Withdrawal of the Centre from health funding
Exclusive provision of health services by the public sector
A larger role for the private sector and NGOs
120.x: NHP 2002 called for more public spending and a larger role for the private sector and NGOs, not exclusive public provision.
xa: The first National Health Policy came in **1983**.
**NHP 2017** adopted an **assurance-based** approach.
NHP 2017 promised **free drugs, diagnostics + emergency care** in public hospitals.

120.s: The National Health Policy, 2017 set a life expectancy target of how many years by 2025?
120.x: NHP 2017 aimed to raise life expectancy from 67.5 to 70 years by 2025, alongside 2.5% of GDP public spending and TFR 2.1.
xa: MMR target: **100 by 2020**.
⚠ The spending target was **missed** — **1.43%** in **2022-23** (NHA).
NHP 2017 is **assurance-based**.

120.s: Under the National Health Policy, 2017, public health spending was targeted at what share of GDP by 2025?
120.x: NHP 2017 targeted public health spending of 2.5% of GDP by 2025; it was missed, at 1.43% in 2022-23.

120.s:
Consider the following statements about the National Health Policy, 2017 targets:
1. Total fertility rate of 2.1 by 2025.
2. Public health spending of 1.43% of GDP by 2025.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
120.x: NHP 2017 set a TFR of 2.1 by 2025. Its spending target was 2.5% of GDP; 1.43% is the level actually reached in 2022-23.

120.s: In which of the following years was the National Rural Health Mission launched, to ensure accessible, affordable, and quality healthcare for the rural population?
120.src: APPSC 2023 Lecturers in Government Degree Colleges

120.s: Which scheme entitles pregnant women to free ('zero expense') delivery and newborn care at public facilities?
120.x: JSSK is the free-entitlement scheme; JSY gives cash assistance for institutional delivery and is 100% centrally sponsored.
xa: AP JSY: **1,76,966** beneficiaries (Apr-Dec **2024**).
**RKSK** covers adolescents **10-19 years**.
NHM funding: **60:40**; NE and Himalayan states **90:10**.

120.s: The usual Centre–State funding pattern under the National Health Mission is:
o: 60:40, with 90:10 for North-Eastern and Himalayan States
120.x: The normal funding pattern is 60:40 between the Centre and States, while North-Eastern and Himalayan States receive a 90:10 pattern.
120.tq: Compare the general funding ratio with the special ratio for specified regions.
xs: NHM funding: **Centre:State 60:40**, **90:10** for **NE and Himalayan states** — option **(3)**.
⚠ **JSY** is **100%** centrally sponsored.
xa: NRHM aims at **accessible, affordable, quality care** for rural India.
ASHAs + ANMs form the **backbone of rural care**.

120.s: The Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (RKSK) covers adolescents aged:
120.x: RKSK covers 10-19 year-olds through Adolescent Friendly Health Clinics, weekly iron folic acid supplementation and peer educators.
xa: RKSK also covers **menstrual hygiene**.
**Anaemia Mukt Bharat** (2018) follows the **6x6x6** strategy.

120.s: Which of the following pairs relating to ASHA is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Level of work – Block-level medical officer
Role – Link between households and the health system
Level of work – Village-level community health worker
120.x: ASHA is a village-level community health worker who, with the ANM, links rural households to the health system; she is not a block-level medical officer.
xa: **Mobile Academy** is an audio course for ASHAs.
ASHAs came under **NRHM** (**2005**).

120.s: Anaemia Mukt Bharat was launched in:
120.x: Anaemia Mukt Bharat was launched in 2018 and follows the 6x6x6 strategy; 2014 is wrong.

120.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Mobile Academy – Weekly audio messages to mothers
120.x: JSY gives cash for institutional delivery. JSSK gives free delivery, RKSK covers adolescents of 10–19 years, and Mobile Academy is an audio course for ASHAs (Kilkari sends messages to mothers).

120.s: Which National Health Mission scheme gives cash assistance for institutional delivery?
120.x: Janani Suraksha Yojana gives cash for institutional delivery and is 100% centrally sponsored; JSSK gives free, zero-expense delivery.

120.s: Under the National Health Mission, the Centre–State funding ratio for North-Eastern and Himalayan States is:
120.x: NHM funding is usually 60:40, but 90:10 for North-Eastern and Himalayan States.

120.s: Mission Indradhanush aims at what level of full immunisation?
120.x: The December 2014 catch-up drive under UIP for zero-dose and partly immunised children targets 90% full immunisation.
xa: **U-WIN** digitises maternal and child vaccination records.
**MR-1** at **9-12 months** is the correct PYQ pair.

120.s: Which one of the following sets of vaccines is administered at birth under the Universal Immunisation Programme?
o: BCG, OPV-0 and Hepatitis B birth dose
MR-2, DPT booster-1 and OPV booster
Td, DPT booster-2 and Rotavirus vaccine
120.x: The birth schedule includes BCG, OPV-0 and the birth dose of Hepatitis B.
120.tq: Start with the age column and eliminate vaccines belonging to later schedules.
xs: At birth: **BCG, OPV-0 and Hepatitis B birth dose** — option **(1)**.
**MR-1, JE-1, PCV booster** = **9-12 months**; **MR-2, DPT booster-1, OPV booster** = **16-24 months**; **Td** = **10 and 16 years**.
xa: **6, 10, 14 weeks**: OPV 1-3, Pentavalent 1-3, Rotavirus, fIPV; **PCV** at 6 and 14 weeks.
**DPT booster-2**: **5-6 years**.
Mission Indradhanush targets **90%** full immunisation.

120.s: Under the Universal Immunisation Programme schedule, which one of the following vaccine-age pairs is correctly matched?
120.x: MR-1 is given at 9-12 months (the correct PYQ pair). Td is given at 10 and 16 years, not 5-6 years; OPV-1 is given at 6 weeks, not 16-24 months (when the OPV booster is given); DPT booster-2 is given at 5-6 years, not 6 weeks.
120.tq: MR-1 at 9-12 months; Td at 10 and 16 years; DPT booster-2 at 5-6 years.
xs: **MR-1 — 9-12 months** is correct — option **(1)** (correct PYQ pair).
**Td** is at **10 and 16 years**, not 5-6 years.
**OPV-1** is at **6 weeks**; at **16-24 months** comes the **OPV booster**.
**DPT booster-2** is at **5-6 years**, not 6 weeks.
xa: At 9-12 months also: **JE-1** (endemic districts), **PCV booster**, **Vitamin A**.
**16-24 months**: **MR-2**, DPT booster-1, OPV booster, **JE-2**.

120.s: Under the Universal Immunisation Programme, the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) primary doses are given at:
120.x: PCV is given at 6 and 14 weeks, with a booster at 9-12 months.

120.s: Under the UIP schedule, Td (tetanus and adult diphtheria) is given at:
120.x: Td is given at 10 and 16 years; at 5–6 years it is DPT booster-2, a common trap.

120.s: U-WIN is a digital registry for:
o: Routine immunisation of pregnant women and children
120.x: U-WIN is the digital registry of routine immunisation for pregnant women and children.

120.s: Mission Indradhanush, launched in December 2014, mainly reaches:
120.x: Mission Indradhanush is a catch-up drive under UIP for zero-dose and partly immunised children, targeting 90% full immunisation.

120.s: Which pillar of Ayushman Bharat provides comprehensive primary care?
120.x: Ayushman Arogya Mandirs provide comprehensive primary care. PM-JAY is the hospitalisation assurance pillar, ABDM the digital backbone and PM-ABHIM the health infrastructure pillar.

120.s: Primary care, delivered through Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, is expected to meet about what share of health needs?
120.x: Primary care meets 80-90% of health needs; the AAM target was 1,50,000 centres and over 1.73 lakh have been converted.
xa: AAM services: NCD screening (hypertension, diabetes, **oral/breast/cervix** cancers), mental health, ENT, eye, geriatric, palliative + trauma care.
Campaigns: **Ayushman Sabhas**, weekly **Ayushman Melas**, **Ayushman Gram**.

120.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about PM-ABHIM?
o: It focuses on health infrastructure for pandemics
Its approved outlay of ₹64,180 crore covers FY 2016–17 to FY 2020–21
It was launched on 25 October 2021 at Varanasi
It includes critical care blocks, Integrated Public Health Laboratories and BSL-3 laboratories
120.x: The ₹64,180 crore outlay covers FY 2021–22 to FY 2025–26.
xa: In AP, **J.P. Nadda** inaugurated **10 Critical Care Blocks and 12 IPHLs** (**₹250 crore**) from **Vijayawada** (13 Sep 2026).
The other Ayushman Bharat pillars: **Ayushman Arogya Mandir** and **ABDM**.

120.s: PM-ABHIM was launched on 25 October 2021 at:
120.x: The Prime Minister launched PM-ABHIM at Varanasi on 25 October 2021.

120.s: The outlay of PM-ABHIM (2021-22 to 2025-26) is:
120.x: PM-ABHIM has an outlay of ₹64,180 crore, the largest pan-India health infrastructure scheme.

120.s: The target for Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (earlier AB-HWCs) was:
120.x: The target was 1,50,000; over 1.73 lakh have been converted.

120.s: ABHA, the health ID under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission, has how many digits?
120.x: ABHA is a 14-digit health ID; accounts crossed 90 crore by June 2026.
xa: Earlier (Aug 2025): **79.91 crore** accounts; **67.19 crore** linked records.
**NMC (Mar 2026)**: all medical colleges to link ABHA IDs for OPD/IPD/emergency patients.

120.s: The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission is implemented by:
120.x: ABDM, launched in September 2021, is implemented by the National Health Authority, not NITI Aayog.

120.s: The March 2026 direction of the National Medical Commission required medical colleges to generate and link ABHA IDs for:
o: All OPD, IPD and emergency patients
120.x: The NMC directed medical colleges to generate and link ABHA IDs for all OPD, IPD and emergency patients, partly to detect fake patients during inspections.
120.tq: Identify the complete beneficiary category rather than narrowing the order to one department or scheme.
xs: **NMC (Mar 2026)** ordered medical colleges to generate and link **ABHA IDs** for **all OPD, IPD and emergency patients** — option **(2)**.
The aim: **weed out fake patients** during inspections.
xa: ABHA is a **14-digit** health ID; **90 crore+** accounts (Jun 2026).
Aug 2025: **79.91 crore** accounts, **67.19 crore** linked records.
AP's **Sanjeevani** gives an ABHA ID to every citizen.

120.s: Arogya Mitra, sometimes confused with ABDM components, actually belongs to:

120.s: Which ABDM component is meant for testing?
120.x: The Sandbox is ABDM's testing component; UHI and the Consent Manager are gateways and the Drug Registry is a registry.

120.s: Which of the following is NOT one of the four principal registries of ABDM?
120.x: The four registries are ABHA, Healthcare Professionals Registry, Health Facility Registry and Drug Registry. Arogya Mitra is not an ABDM component.

xs: **Arogya Mitra registry** is not an ABDM registry — option **(1)**; Arogya Mitra is a **PM-JAY hospital facilitator** (APPSC 2025 PYQ).
The four registries: **ABHA**, **Healthcare Professionals Registry**, **Health Facility Registry** and **Drug Registry**.
xa: ABHA is a **14-digit** ID; **90 crore+** accounts (Jun 2026).
ABDM is run by the **National Health Authority**.
Gateways: **Consent Manager**, **UHI**, **NHCX**.

120.s: The Eat Right India campaign (2018) was launched by:

xa: FSSAI was created under the **Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006**.
Eat Right India + Fit India together aim to **cut NCD deaths**.
**ICMR** began in **1911** as **IRFA**; renamed in **1949**.

120.s: The Eat Right India and Fit India campaigns together seek to reduce deaths due to:
120.x: Together, Eat Right India and Fit India aim to reduce deaths caused by non-communicable diseases through healthier diets and increased physical activity.
120.tq: Infer the common public-health outcome from the two campaigns’ complementary objectives.
xs: Eat Right India and Fit India together aim to cut **non-communicable disease (NCD)** deaths — option **(1)**.
Eat Right India promotes healthy diets; **Fit India** fights **sedentary lifestyles**.
xa: Fit India: **2019**; Eat Right India: **2018** (FSSAI).
**India Hypertension Control Initiative** is an ICMR consortium.

120.s: The Fit India Movement was launched in:
120.x: Fit India Movement began in 2019 to bring fitness into daily life; Swachh Bharat was 2014 and Eat Right India 2018.

120.s: FSSAI, which runs Eat Right India, was created under the:
120.x: FSSAI was created under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.

120.s:
Indian Council for Medical Research (ICMR) developed the strategic plan and Vision 2030 document based on the following:

I. Strengthen health research capacity in the country

II. Leverage traditional medicine

III. Well aligned with the National Health Policy NHP-2017
Select the correct answer from below:
Which of the following is an ICMR-related initiative?
120.x: The India TB Research Consortium is listed among ICMR initiatives, with MERA India and the India Hypertension Control Initiative. India Food Security Consortium is not an ICMR initiative; Eat Right India is FSSAI's and U-WIN is the immunisation registry.

120.s: How many pillars does ICMR's Strategic Plan 2017-24 ('Vision 2030') have?
120.x: Vision 2030 has 5 pillars and 15 goals.

120.s: Which of the following is NOT a pillar of ICMR's 'Vision 2030' strategic plan?
120.x: The five pillars are capacity building, data management, leveraging traditional medicine, evidence to policy, and strengthening programme implementation through research; health insurance is not one.

120.s: The Indian Research Fund Association was renamed ICMR in:
120.x: IRFA, set up in 1911, was renamed ICMR in 1949.

Who is the present Director General of World Health Organization?
The World Health Organization's member count in April, 1991 was :
120.x: The World Health Organization had a membership of 166 in April, 1991. Its membership in the year 2009 was 193. It was founded in April, 1948 and is headquartered in Geneva. Its membership in the year 2013 increased to 194.

120.s: When was World Health Organization (W.H.O.) established?
120.x: WHO’s Constitution came into force on 7 April 1948 – a date we now celebrate every year as World Health Day.

120.s: World Health Day is observed on 7 April every year because on that date in 1948:
o: the World Health Organization was founded, with its headquarters at Geneva
the Alma-Ata Declaration on primary health care was adopted
the World Health Organization was founded, with its headquarters at New York
smallpox was declared eradicated by the World Health Assembly
120.x: WHO was founded on 7 April 1948 and is headquartered at Geneva, so World Health Day falls on 7 April. WHO's headquarters is not New York; the Alma-Ata Declaration and the eradication of smallpox are later events and not linked to 7 April 1948.
120.tq: WHO: Geneva, 7 April 1948 = World Health Day.
xs: **WHO** was founded on **7 April 1948**, headquartered at **Geneva** — option **(1)**.
Hence **World Health Day is 7 April**; WHO's headquarters is not New York.
xa: ⚠ **1949** is when IRFA was renamed **ICMR**.
ICMR's origin: **IRFA**, **1911**.
**One of the oldest** medical research bodies is ICMR.

120.s:
Consider the following statements about the World Health Organization:
1. Its headquarters is at Geneva.
2. Its membership reached 194 in 2013.
3. The second term of its Director-General ends in 2025.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
120.x: WHO is at Geneva and has had 194 members since 2013. Tedros's second term ends on 15 August 2027, not 2025.

120.s: The theme of World Health Day 2026 is:
o: Together for health. Stand with science
120.x: World Health Day 2026 theme is 'Together for health. Stand with science'.

120.s: The Sanjeevani digital health programme of Andhra Pradesh, commencing in August 2026, is primarily associated with which of the following?
o: Replacement of all public hospitals by private hospitals
Universal distribution of fortified food through fair-price shops
Free insurance cover of ₹5 lakh for every citizen
A digital health profile and ABHA ID for every citizen
120.x: Sanjeevani aims to create a digital health profile and ABHA ID for every citizen of Andhra Pradesh.
120.tq: Identify the defining feature of the programme rather than confusing it with an insurance scheme.
xs: AP's **Sanjeevani** (from **Aug 2026**) gives a **digital health profile and ABHA ID for every citizen** — option **(4)**.
It does not privatise hospitals, distribute food or give a fixed insurance cover.
xa: It links PHCs, hospitals, labs, **e-Aushadhi**, **108**, **104**, telemedicine + **AI assistance**.
The **Sanjeevani Citizen Wellness App** came in **Jul 2026**.
It makes AP an **ABDM-linked**, citizen-wide digital health state.

120.s: In Andhra Pradesh, telemedicine services are available in:
o: Only private hospitals empanelled under PM-JAY
None of the Ayushman Arogya Mandirs
120.x: Telemedicine is available in all Ayushman Arogya Mandirs in Andhra Pradesh (APPSC 2024); it is not confined to AIIMS Mangalagiri or empanelled private hospitals.
